definition: Dask scales NumPy, pandas and plain Python code to datasets bigger than memory and to clusters of machines.
details: Created by Matthew Rocklin at Anaconda in 2014; now community maintained, with commercial support from Coiled.

explainer.lead: How to install Dask, a first working example, and where it fits in an AI project.
explainer.createdBy: Created by Matthew Rocklin at Anaconda; community maintained.

quickstart.python:
import dask.dataframe as dd

df = dd.read_parquet("logs/*.parquet")      # many files, lazily
daily = df.groupby("day")["tokens"].sum()
print(daily.compute())                       # runs in parallel

explainer.inAi: Use Dask to preprocess large corpora or run many model predictions in parallel without rewriting pandas code.
explainer.jsNote: Dask is a Python library with no official JavaScript or TypeScript package; call it from a Python service if your app is written in JavaScript.

tiers.eli5: Instead of one person carrying every box, you split the boxes into labelled piles and a coordinator hands them out to a crew, then reassembles the results.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use Dask to parallelise pandas or NumPy workflows and to scale them across a cluster. A common pitfall is treating it as a drop-in pandas replacement: lazy evaluation and partitioning mean careful choice of chunk sizes and avoiding operations that pull everything into memory.
tiers.paperLevel: Dask represents computation as a task graph of delayed operations over partitioned arrays and DataFrames, scheduled lazily across cores or nodes. Limits: performance depends on partition sizing and data locality, and not all pandas or NumPy APIs are supported.

explainer.example: A 500 GB Parquet dataset is read into a Dask DataFrame split into many partitions, filtered and grouped, and only the small aggregated result is computed and collected.
